cue.topic: Describe a time you helped someone
bullets: and explain how you felt afterwards

part2.model: I'd like to talk about the time I helped my elderly neighbour, Mrs Okoro, who is in her seventies and lives alone. It happened last winter, when a severe storm knocked out the power across our whole street. I knew she would be struggling in the dark, so I grabbed a torch and went straight over to check on her. She was visibly shaken, and she couldn't find her medicine because the hallway was pitch black. I helped her track down her tablets, then I fetched some blankets and heated soup on our gas stove. She kept thanking me, which made me feel a bit embarrassed, because anyone would have done the same. Honestly, I was glad I happened to be home that night. I ended up staying with her for about three hours until the electricity finally came back on. The reason she needed help was simple. Her family live abroad, and she isn't confident with a smartphone, so she had no way of calling anyone. Before leaving, I wrote my number on a card and stuck it beside her phone in case of emergencies. Afterwards it felt incredibly rewarding, to be honest. It wasn't a grand gesture, but she was so grateful that she cried a little. That evening made me realise how a small act of kindness can strengthen the bond between neighbours, and we've been much closer ever since.

vocab.example: I'll pop round to check on my grandfather after work.

vocab.example: The driver was visibly shaken after the near miss on the motorway.

vocab.meaning: completely dark with no light at all
vocab.example: The forest was pitch black once the sun had gone down.

vocab.meaning: a caring action done to help someone else

Personally, I believe schools and families should encourage generosity much earlier, so that it becomes second nature. Over time, that habit could change a whole community.

questions.q: In what ways has the internet changed the way people give to charity?
questions.model: It has made giving far quicker and easier. Crowdfunding platforms, for instance, allow thousands of strangers to raise funds for a sick child within days, and social media helps appeals go viral. On the other hand, some argue that clicking a donate button is rather impersonal and may replace face-to-face support for those in need. Personally, I think the best approach is to combine both, so that technology supports genuine human contact.

questions.model: Both are valuable, but I'd lean towards giving time. Money is useful, yet it can disappear into administration costs, whereas volunteering creates direct, visible change. Spending a weekend teaching kids to read, for example, can transform a life in a way a small donation rarely does, and it builds lasting relationships. Ideally, people should do a bit of both, depending on their circumstances and what is most needed. Giving your time also shows people that someone genuinely cares.

questions.q: Should the government or individuals be responsible for helping people in need?
questions.model: Ideally it should be a shared responsibility. Governments have the resources to provide a safety net, such as healthcare and unemployment benefits, which charities simply cannot match. However, individuals fill the gaps by offering personal, flexible support. So I believe a combination of both works best for any healthy society. Without that balance, vulnerable people could easily slip through the cracks. In my experience, countries that combine both approaches seem noticeably fairer and more stable overall.

I've seen this work well in my old school, where pupils still volunteer long after they graduate.
